You may follow him at Twitter @FidelRahmati A large-scale Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions killed at least 17 people and injured more than 40, prompting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to warn that delays in replacing Patriot air defense interceptors are costing civilian lives. Russia launched one of its largest overnight aerial assaults on Ukraine, firing dozens of ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles alongside 168 drones, Ukraine’s Air Force said on Thursday. Reuters reported on August 20 that Ukrainian air defenses intercepted around 90% of the drones and most cruise missiles, but failed to shoot down any of the ballistic missiles used in the attack. Ukrainian officials say Patriot systems remain the country’s only effective defense against ballistic missile strikes. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the deadliest strike hit the capital’s Solomianskyi district, where the upper floors of a nine-story residential building were destroyed. Most of the fatalities were reported from that building. Authorities said the attacks also damaged a school, a children’s hospital, warehouses and several non-residential buildings across Kyiv, while emergency crews continued search-and-rescue operations through the rubble. Russia also struck the Black Sea region of Odesa, continuing a series of attacks on Ukraine’s port infrastructure. Repeated strikes on ports and cargo facilities in recent weeks have severely disrupted Ukraine’s agricultural exports, raising concerns over global food supplies. In a separate development, Romania’s Ministry of Defense said a Russian drone crashed inside Romanian territory during the attacks. Romania, a NATO and European Union member, said it is investigating the incident. Following the latest barrage, Zelenskiy renewed his appeal for Ukraine’s allies to urgently replenish stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles. “Patriot interceptors have still not been replaced, even though we need them every day,” Zelenskiy wrote on Telegram. “Every additional interceptor missile saves lives.” He argued that Russia would not engage in meaningful peace negotiations as long as Ukraine lacks sufficient missile defense capabilities to protect its cities, adding that the international response has not matched the scale of Russia’s attacks. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen echoed Zelenskiy’s call, describing Ukraine’s defense against ballistic missiles as the bloc’s “most urgent priority.” She said the European Union is working with member states and partners to strengthen Kyiv’s air defense capabilities. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and large-scale missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian cities have continued throughout the war. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxly.text: Image source, Reuters By Mansur Abubakar Reporting from Abuja Published 14 September 2026, 16:47 BST Updated 4 hours ago Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote has launched Africa's largest ever share sale, offering a stake in his oil refinery to the general public in a deal that could raise as much as $2.1bn (Â£1.6bn). The initial public offering (IPO) is for roughly 3% of the Dangote refinery, with the billionaire saying he wanted to give ordinary Nigerians the chance to share in the plant's success. The refinery, which started production in 2024, is one of the largest in the world and took more than a decade to complete. It now supplies more than 70% of Nigeria's energy consumption, and many Nigerians have expressed excitement at the prospect of owning a part of it. Among them is Isah Salisu, who told the BBC he withdrew 50,000 naira (Â£28; $37) from his savings to invest. "My hope is that my small money will one day grow big. I don't want to miss out as many I know are also investing," he said. The IPO lasts for a month and the minimum purchase is 10 shares, costing about $4. Economy and business expert Dr Abdulrazak Ibrahim Fagge told the BBC that Monday's event was historic. But he warned investors that the price of the shares could fall, meaning people could lose some of their money. "What prospective buyers, especially first-time buyers, should know is that they shouldn't invest all their money or money they would need in a couple of months," he said. "They should invest something they could do without for the next three, four, five years." He also warned people to be wary of scammers, saying there are people who would want to take advantage of those without good knowledge of the process. "I will advise people to only deal with the institutions that have been listed," he said. Nigeria is Africa's biggest oil producer but until the refinery was opened, most of the country's fuel had to be imported because of a lack of refining capacity in the country. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The refinery, which opened in 2024, is one of the largest in the world Born in Kano, Dangote, 67, has a net worth of around $28bn, according to Forbes magazine. He made his fortune in cement and sugar in Nigeria before expanding to 16 other African countries. His company Dangote Cement is Africa's largest cement producer. The Lagos refinery was first announced in 2013 with an initial estimated cost of around $19bn, but construction did not begin until 2017. It was further delayed by the Covid-19 pandemic. The site, in the Lekki Free Zone near Lagos, required massive land reclamation, with 65 million cubic metres of sand moved. The refinery has a processing capacity of 650,000 barrels per day, making it the seventh-largest in the world. The money raised by the share offer is intended to help double its capacity. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/16/kenn.text: Most of the Kennedy Centre in Washington, DC will close for repairs following a board vote Tuesday, hours after a federal judge again blocked the landmark venue from being renamed after President Donald Trump.“Simply put, Defendants cannot install memorials for President Trump or anyone or anything else at the Kennedy Center without Congress’s blessing,” US District Judge Christopher Cooper said in the latest ruling Tuesday.Trump, in response to the ruling, said the $257 million (€223 million) allocated by Congress for the repairs would only be released if renaming was permitted. Federal courts have twice ruled cannot be met without Congressional approval.Judge Cooper ruled in May that the Kennedy Center illegally added Trump’s name to the building, ordering it removed. The institution’s leaders complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding in place where Trump’s name was once displayed.The Justice Department has appealed the latest ruling.Trump, who was named the Kennedy Centre’s chairman last year by loyalists on the board, participated in the virtual board meeting and said on social media he’d given $17 million to an endowment intended to support the institution.The meeting included testy exchanges at points between Trump and Rep. Joyce Beatty, an Ohio Democrat who has led the campaign to block efforts to memorialise the president at the Kennedy Centre.Fans worry about possible demolitionThe developments have thrown into limbo the fate of one of the US's most prominent cultural institutions, a place where presidents, lawmakers and celebrities of all political ideologies have gathered for decades to recognise and celebrate the best in American arts and culture.The venue’s leaders have long argued that the building, which began construction in 1965, was in dire need of renovations. A partial ceiling collapse in the building’s main hallway earlier this month intensified the calls for renovations.“The building is not currently built to last; the chairman knows that because he is among the best builders in the world,” Brian Ballard, Kennedy Centre board member, said in a statement.But Trump’s insistence on a physical recognition of his work, reminiscent of his tendency to add his name to buildings as a real estate developer, has been a persistent sticking point.It's the latest setback in Trump’s second-term bid to dramatically remake the US capital in his gilded tastes. He’s demolished the East Wing of the White House and is replacing it with a ballroom and plans to build a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery. He’s also eyeing a golf course renovation along the Potomac River.The Kennedy Centre board voted in August to inscribe his name on the Kennedy Centre’s facade so it would read “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” If the Trump Kennedy Centre Fund reached $100 million, (approximately €86.66 million), another inscription would be added reading “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.”The plaza in front of the Kennedy Centre would also be renamed in Trump’s honour.There are concerns that the administration may seek to demolish the Kennedy Center. According to a filing last month, administration lawyers told the court that absent recognition of the president, the Kennedy Center would struggle to raise money for renovations.Without that money, they suggested, the building may need to be demolished.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckre.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, Witkoff and Zelensky met in the Norwegian capital By Paul Adams Diplomatic correspondent Published 1 hour ago The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky ahead of this afternoon's talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country. Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!" But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner? The two men have never been close â that much is obvious â but have they now fallen out once and for all? Both in rhetoric and actions, the past ten days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship. Just listen to the way they talk about each other. "Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week. The verbal assault has continued this week. "Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously. In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu "has no f**king judgement". Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister". "Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad." Figure caption, Watch: Zelensky says US military intelligence sharing "works now" For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart. But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us." Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever. "We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday. But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship? In some ways, we've been here before. After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing. The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead. One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles. Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks. Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports â not confirmed by US officials â come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv. Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel. Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv. Figure caption, Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin. "What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks applied to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC. "It's inexplicable and saddening." Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment". For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025. Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation â again not confirmed by Washington â that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service. Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking. "We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News. On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded. The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings. Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink . A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones. Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones. It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink â or its military grade equivalent Starshield â originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House. Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet." But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations. Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular. Image source, EPA Image caption, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued unabated A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine. When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference. During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused. At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (Â£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment. Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip. Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin. Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things." "There's nothing to gain fromâ¦ digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically. Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink. "I think we will have good results too," he said. Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.
